bib.title: MEDUSA: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Vienna, Austria. PMLR 235, 2024

question: Can extra decoding heads on the LLM's own last hidden state, verified with tree attention, speed up decoding without a separate draft model?
hypothesis: Multiple lightweight heads plus tree attention avoid the draft-model problems of speculative decoding and reduce decoding steps while keeping quality.
contributions: MEDUSA heads with tree attention for parallel candidate verification
MEDUSA-1 (frozen backbone) and MEDUSA-2 (joint training) recipes
Self-distillation for when training data is unavailable or the model went through RLHF
Typical acceptance scheme as an alternative to rejection sampling

method.summary: K feed-forward heads (one layer with residual, W2 initialised from the LM head, W1 zero) are added on the last hidden state; top-s_k predictions per head form a Cartesian-product (or greedily optimised sparse) candidate tree verified in one pass with a tree attention mask. Heads are trained on a frozen backbone (MEDUSA-1) or jointly with LoRA/QLoRA plus combined loss, differential LR and warmup (MEDUSA-2).

datasets.name: Self-distilled data (ShareGPT + UltraChat seeds)
datasets.source: generated by Vicuna-33B (random sampling, temperature 0.3) and Zephyr-7B (self-talk)

datasets.name: MT-Bench
datasets.split: 8 categories; writing and roleplay for ablations

datasets.name: AlpacaEval
datasets.source: Li et al., 2023; also used to estimate head accuracies for tree search

models.name: Vicuna-33B
models.architecture: Llama chat, experimental, private training data

models.name: MEDUSA heads
models.architecture: 5 heads, 1 layer each: softmax(W2(SiLU(W1 h)+h)), W1 dxd, W2 dxV
models.init_from: W2 from LM head, W1 zero

training.objective: MEDUSA-1: sum_k -lambda_k log p^(k)(y_{t+k+1}), lambda_k=0.8^k. MEDUSA-2: L_LM + lambda0 * L_MEDUSA-1. Self-distill: KL(p_original||p) for backbone.
training.lr: Vicuna 7B/13B MEDUSA-2: peak 5e-4 backbone, 2e-3 heads; self-distill: 1e-4 backbone LoRA; heads 4x backbone LR
training.lr_schedule: cosine with warmup; sine schedule on lambda0 for self-distillation
training.regularisation: LoRA rank 32, alpha 16 on all linear layers incl. LM head
training.hardware: single NVIDIA A100 PCIE (7B MEDUSA-1 timing)
training.wall_clock: about 5 hours for MEDUSA-1 Vicuna-7B on 60k ShareGPT samples

other.stage_note: Vicuna 7B/13B: MEDUSA-1 first, then used as init for MEDUSA-2 with QLoRA; Vicuna-33B/Zephyr: MEDUSA-2 directly with LoRA (unquantized recommended)

inference.decoding: candidate tree from top-s_k of each head, tree attention verification; rejection sampling or typical acceptance
inference.temperature: 0.7 for typical-acceptance ablation (Fig 5); 0.3 for generating Vicuna-33B self-distillation data; main speed tables: not stated

parameters.typical_acceptance: accept if p_orig > min(eps, delta*exp(-H)); alpha = sqrt(eps); eps swept 0.01 to 0.25 step 0.01; first token greedy
parameters.tree: sparse tree of 64 nodes, depth 4 for Vicuna-7B MEDUSA-2; built greedily from head top-i accuracies on calibration data (AlpacaEval)

other.spec_decoding_drafts: Llama-68M, Llama-160M, Tiny-Llama (1B), Tiny-Vicuna; best gamma 4 (7B), 3 (13B), 3 (33B); torch.compile on drafts
other.hardware_for_speed: not stated for main results (A100-80GB PCIe used in App G)

metrics.name: Acceleration rate
metrics.definition: average tokens decoded per decoding step

metrics.name: Overhead
metrics.definition: average per-step latency of MEDUSA model divided by that of vanilla model

baselines: speculative decoding with open-source draft models
direct fine-tuning of backbone with heads
eval.protocol: Batch size 1; MT-Bench with GPT-4 judge; no seeds or confidence intervals reported.

evidence.quote: peak learning rate of 5e−4 for the backbone and 2e−3 for MEDUSA heads

results.claim: MEDUSA-1 gives 2.18x speedup on Vicuna-7B with no quality loss.
results.setup: Vicuna-7B v1.5, ShareGPT-trained heads, MT-Bench, batch size 1, HuggingFace baseline
results.quote: MEDUSA-1 shows a 2.18× speedup, while MEDUSA-2 further improves this to a 2.83×.
results.note: Abstract says MEDUSA-1 achieves 'over 2.2x'; Sec 3.1, Fig 3a and Table 2 give 2.18x for 7B (2.33x for 13B).

results.setup: Vicuna-7B v1.5, ShareGPT-trained heads, MT-Bench, batch size 1, HuggingFace baseline
results.quote: MEDUSA-1 shows a 2.18× speedup, while MEDUSA-2 further improves this to a 2.83×.

results.claim: MEDUSA-1 gives 2.33x speedup on Vicuna-13B; MEDUSA-2 2.83x.
results.quote: MEDUSA-1 results in a 2.33× speed increase

results.claim: Self-distilled MEDUSA-2 on Vicuna-33B reaches only 2.35x speedup (acc rate 3.01, overhead 1.27), quality +0.05 on MT-Bench.
results.setup: Vicuna-33B, ~100k self-distilled samples, MT-Bench, GPT-4 judge

results.claim: Speculative decoding with open-source draft models gets 1.47x on Vicuna-7B, 1.56x on 13B, 1.60x on 33B, below MEDUSA-2 on 7B/13B.
results.table: Table 1, row SSpecDecoding, columns Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B, Vicuna-33B

results.claim: Per-category speedup for MEDUSA-2 Vicuna-7B peaks at 3.62x on Extraction and 3.29x on Coding.
results.quote: The “Extraction” category shows the highest speedup at 3.62×

results.claim: Direct fine-tuning of the backbone with the heads degrades MT-Bench quality (5.925 vs 6.17 baseline), while MEDUSA-1 gets 6.23 and MEDUSA-2 6.18.
results.table: Table 2, column Direct Fine-tuning, row Quality

results.claim: Speedup ladder: heads without tree attention ~1.5x, with tree attention ~1.9x, optimized tree ~2.2x, MEDUSA-2 ~2.8x.
results.table: Table 3, rows Medusa-1 heads without tree attention through Training heads with Medusa-2

results.claim: A sparse optimized tree with 64 nodes gets a better acceleration rate than a dense tree with 256 nodes.
results.setup: MEDUSA-2 Vicuna-7B, MT-Bench writing and roleplay
results.quote: The sparse tree configuration with 64 nodes shows a better acceleration rate than the dense tree settings with 256 nodes.

results.claim: Training MEDUSA-1 on Vicuna-7B takes about 5 hours on one A100 PCIE over 60k ShareGPT samples.
results.quote: 5 hours for MEDUSA-1 on Vicuna 7B model with a single NVIDIA A100 PCIE GPU to train on 60k ShareGPT samples

results.claim: Raising the typical-acceptance threshold epsilon raises quality and lowers acceleration rate; typical acceptance is comparable to random sampling at large epsilon.
results.setup: MEDUSA-2 Vicuna-7B, MT-Bench writing/roleplay, temperature 0.7, epsilon 0.01 to 0.25 step 0.01
results.quote: as ϵ increases, there is an elevation in quality at the expense of a reduced acceleration rate.

results.claim: Simulation: speedup falls past ~64 candidate tokens and when batch size exceeds 32 as linear layers become compute-bound.
results.setup: Simplified Llama-7B block, A100 80GB PCIe, seq len 1024, analytic model acc rate = 0.477 log(num candidate)
results.quote: when the batch size exceeds 32, the speedup decreases and may even have a negative effect

limits: Main experiments are batch size 1 only; larger batch handled only by simulation (App G) and a remark that TensorRT and TGI support it.
Self-distilled models (Vicuna-13B/33B, Zephyr) get lower speedup than ShareGPT-trained ones; authors hypothesise dataset mismatch for Vicuna-33B.
Typical acceptance does not preserve the original output distribution (authors say matching it is unnecessary).
No seeds, variance or hardware for main speed results stated; no code or weights link in the text.
Speculative-decoding baselines use open-source draft models, not the proprietary originals.

terms.definition: the average number of tokens decoded per decoding step
per decoding step overhead compared to classic decoding, average per step latency of the MEDUSA models divided by that of the vanilla model
wall-time acceleration rate = acceleration rate / overhead
